linq.title: LINQ for Java · PiscesCup
linq.description: LINQ for Java: an Enumerable query library for Java 25, featuring fluent queries, deferred execution and primitive-specialized sequences.
linq.lead: Inspired by .NET LINQ, bringing fluent, deferred-execution sequence queries to Java 25 collections and primitive streams.
linq.overview: LINQ for Java provides queries for Java collections and sequences through the Enumerable model. Methods such as where, select and orderBy compose data processing steps; many intermediate operations use deferred execution and run when results are enumerated or consumed.
linq.enumerablesIntro: Object sequences and specialized int, long and double sequences provide query entry points for the corresponding data types.
linq.objectDescription: Create sequences from arrays, collections or varargs, then filter, order, group and join objects.
linq.intDescription: Use Linq.ofInts for int-specific queries and numeric aggregation such as sum and average.
linq.longDescription: Use Linq.ofLongs for long-valued data, reducing unnecessary boxing and unboxing in primitive pipelines.
linq.doubleDescription: Use Linq.ofDoubles for filtering, transforming and aggregating double-valued data.
linq.features.filterDescription: Filter elements with where, transform results with select, and control sequence ranges with skip and take.
linq.features.orderDescription: Combine orderBy and thenBy for multi-level sorting, and use groupBy to group elements by key.
linq.features.joinDescription: Correlate sequences with join and groupJoin; use distinct, union, intersect and except for deduplication and set operations.
linq.features.aggregateDescription: Consume results with operators such as count, first and aggregate, or materialize them as lists, arrays and maps.
linq.prepareDescription: The repository README and compiler configuration require JDK 25 or later.
linq.installDescription: Select a build tool and copy the dependency configuration example. Version 1.0.0 is taken from the repository's pom.xml; confirm publication or follow the README to build and install it in a local repository before use.
linq.sampleDescription: Refer to the code examples below to try fluent queries using methods such as where, select, orderBy, and toArray.
linq.relatedDescription: Related projects include the Commons Lib utility dependency and the separate linq-in-java repository.

examples.runHint: Expand an example to view its complete Java class and output. Configure the dependency, save the code with the displayed filename, and run the main method. After selecting a different dependency version, check its compatibility with the version used by the examples.

examples.commons.intro: This section presents five examples adapted from Quick Examples in the Commons Lib README, with main methods and output statements added. Compilation and output were verified with Commons Lib 1.1.6.
examples.commons.namingDescription: Use StringUtils to convert between snake_case, UpperCamel and lowerCamel naming styles.

examples.linq.filterDescription: Create an Int sequence with Linq.ofInts, filter even numbers with where, and retrieve the results with toArray.
examples.linq.projectionDescription: Use select and String::length to map names to their string lengths and collect the results into a List.
examples.linq.orderingDescription: Apply multi-level sorting by age and then name. Person.toString retains the README output format; the optional annotation is omitted.
examples.linq.aggregationDescription: Calculate the sum and average with IntEnumerable's sum and average methods. The example corrects the README output label age to avg.
examples.linq.setsDescription: Use distinct, except, intersect and union for unique values, difference, intersection and union.

tutorial.home.title: Fabric Mod Development Tutorial
tutorial.home.description: Structured coverage of environment configuration, project structure, and development practices for Fabric mods.
chapter00.intro: This chapter presents the configuration workflow for JDK 25, IntelliJ IDEA, and the Fabric mod template, followed by recommended IDEA settings, project file layout, and the implementation of a shared References class.
chapter00.baseline: Note: Localized Chinese UI labels may vary slightly across language pack versions. If a menu entry differs, search Settings directly using the corresponding English label.
chapter00.environment.title: Development environment configuration
chapter00.environment.jdkIntro: The Java Development Kit (JDK) provides both the Java runtime environment and development tools such as the javac compiler. This tutorial targets JDK 25; download and install the full JDK matching your operating system and processor architecture rather than a runtime-only JRE.
chapter00.environment.arch: Select the x64 package for standard Windows systems or the aarch64 package for Apple Silicon macOS devices. After installation, open a new terminal session and run the commands below to verify that both java and javac report major version 25.
chapter00.environment.jdkMismatch: If the reported versions differ, inspect the PATH and JAVA_HOME environment variables. Ensure that JAVA_HOME points to the JDK installation root rather than its bin subdirectory, then reopen the terminal and verify again.
chapter00.environment.ideaIntro: After installing IntelliJ IDEA and opening the template project, configure both Project SDK and Gradle JVM to use the installed JDK 25 via the paths below.
chapter00.environment.ideaRuntime: JetBrains Runtime is used exclusively to run the IDE itself; this section configures the Project SDK for compilation and the Gradle JVM for builds. On macOS, Settings resides under the IntelliJ IDEA application menu, while the remaining paths are identical.
chapter00.environment.generator: Open the official Fabric template generator
chapter00.environment.templateIntro: Select Minecraft 26.3 in the generator and specify the mod name, mod ID, and Java package name. This tutorial uses Vocabulary Spark, vocabulary-spark, and io.github.piscescup.vocabularyspark as reference values. Because the mod ID also serves as the resource namespace, it should be finalized at project creation.
chapter00.environment.templateOptions: Select Java as the programming language, and enable split client sources and data generation as required. Extract the downloaded archive, open the project root directory containing settings.gradle and build.gradle in IntelliJ IDEA, and allow the initial Gradle synchronization to complete.
chapter00.environment.firstRun: Once Gradle synchronization succeeds, execute the command corresponding to your operating system from the project root directory to launch the development client (each command applies to its respective platform and should not be run sequentially):
chapter00.environment.success: A successful launch of the development client confirms that the base environment is properly configured. If startup fails, inspect the error output in the Build tool window or terminal and verify both the JDK configuration and Gradle dependency resolution.
chapter00.settings.title: Recommended IDEA settings
chapter00.settings.intro: Each setting below lists both Chinese and English navigation paths. Visual preferences such as themes and fonts may be tailored to individual preference, whereas file encodings and console encoding are independent settings and must be configured separately.
chapter00.settings.shortcuts: The default shortcut is Ctrl + Alt + S on Windows and Linux, or ⌘ + , on macOS. The search field in the upper-left corner of the dialog allows direct lookup by English setting name if localized labels differ. All paths below begin from this dialog.
chapter00.settings.reopenBody: When enabled, IntelliJ IDEA automatically restores the projects that were open during the previous session. Clear this option to display the welcome screen on startup; this affects startup behavior only.
chapter00.settings.updatesBody: Clearing this option disables automatic IDE update checks and notifications; plugin updates are controlled separately. If IntelliJ IDEA is installed via JetBrains Toolbox, disable automatic tool updates in Toolbox Settings → Tools → Update all tools automatically.
chapter00.settings.themeBody: Configures the overall visual theme of windows, toolbars, and tool panels. Syntax highlighting inside the code editor is configured separately via Color Scheme.
chapter00.settings.uiFontBody: Enable the custom font option to adjust text size across menus, tool windows, and the project tree without affecting the code editor font.
chapter00.settings.backgroundBody: Select a background image and configure its opacity. Enable This project only to restrict the image to the current project. Keep opacity moderate so code contrast remains clear.
chapter00.settings.editor: 2.4 Editor color scheme, font, and comments
chapter00.settings.schemeBody: Controls syntax coloring for keywords, literals, comments, and other code elements. Duplicate any built-in scheme before making modifications.
chapter00.settings.codeFontBody: Sets the default font family and size for the code editor. If the active color scheme defines a scheme-specific font under Color Scheme Font, that setting takes precedence.
chapter00.settings.commentsBody: Select line comments, block comments, or documentation comments to adjust their foreground color. For Java-specific adjustments, navigate to Editor → Color Scheme → Java and clear Inherit values from if required.
chapter00.settings.linesBody: Enabling line numbers is recommended for locating stack traces and compiler diagnostics efficiently. Method separators draw visual dividers between methods and may be enabled as preferred.
chapter00.settings.completionBody: Ensure Show suggestions as you type is enabled, and configure Match case as required. On Windows with the default keymap, Ctrl + Space invokes completion manually.
chapter00.settings.importBody: Enable Add unambiguous imports on the fly so unique symbols are imported automatically, and optionally enable Optimize imports on the fly. Always verify the target package when multiple classes share the same simple name.
chapter00.settings.importReminder: Verify imported package names even with automatic imports enabled. Different Minecraft versions and dependencies may define identically named classes; when candidates are ambiguous, the IDE prompts for explicit selection.
chapter00.settings.encoding: 2.8 Project file encodings: standardize on UTF-8
chapter00.settings.encodingBody: Set Global Encoding, Project Encoding, and Default encoding for properties files to UTF-8, and review the path-override table below to ensure no directory retains a legacy encoding.
chapter00.settings.encodingConvert: For existing files displaying garbled text, select Reload or Convert from the status bar according to the original encoding. Transparent native-to-ascii conversion handles character escaping for .properties files and is distinct from UTF-8 encoding.
chapter00.settings.source.encoding: Project file encodings: standardize on UTF-8
chapter00.settings.consoleBody: Set the default console encoding to UTF-8. This controls how the IDE decodes console streams; if log output remains garbled, verify the actual character encoding emitted by the process or build tool.
chapter00.settings.header: 2.10 File header template for new Java classes
chapter00.settings.headerBody: Configure the File Header template as shown below and replace the author name with your own. The ${NAME} variable is expanded to the class name automatically when a new file is created.
chapter00.settings.headerScope: Selecting Default applies the template across the IDE, whereas Project scopes it to the current project. Confirm that Files → Class includes #parse("File Header.java") only once. Template changes apply solely to newly created files.
chapter00.settings.source.header: File header template for new Java classes
chapter00.plugins.title: Development plugins
chapter00.plugins.intro: After configuring the base environment, install the plugins below as needed. These plugins provide editor-level inspections and navigation, while Gradle continues to manage compilation and project dependencies.
chapter00.plugins.mcdevBody: Provides Minecraft-specific inspections, Mixin assistance, and symbol navigation. Install a version compatible with IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3. Project creation should still use the official Fabric template generator so build scripts remain aligned with the target game release.
chapter00.plugins.ignoreBody: Provides syntax highlighting and editing assistance for .gitignore and similar ignore files. Installation is optional and does not affect Git's native ignore behavior.
chapter00.plugins.languageBody: Simplified Chinese localization is bundled with current IntelliJ IDEA releases and requires no external language pack. If the option is unavailable, verify that Chinese Language Pack is enabled under Plugins → Installed and restart the IDE.
chapter00.files.title: Project files
chapter00.files.intro: Gradle configuration governs the build lifecycle and dependencies, while Fabric directories and metadata declare mod information and entrypoints. The tables below outline the primary files in the Minecraft 26.3 official template.
chapter00.files.gradleRow0: Primary build script declaring the Fabric Loom plugin, Minecraft and Fabric dependencies, compilation settings, and resource processing rules. The Minecraft 26.3 template uses net.fabricmc.fabric-loom.
chapter00.files.gradleRow1: Centralizes version constants and project properties, including minecraft_version, loader_version, fabric_api_version, version, and group.
chapter00.files.gradleRow2: Defines the root project name and Gradle plugin-resolution repositories.
chapter00.files.gradleRow3: Pins the Gradle distribution version used by the project. Use the bundled Gradle Wrapper rather than a separate global installation.
chapter00.files.gradleRow4: Gradle Wrapper launcher scripts: gradlew on macOS and Linux, and gradlew.bat on Windows.
chapter00.files.gradleRow5: Local build caches and compiled output directories; exclude them from version control.
chapter00.files.fabricRow0: Contains common Java source code, including the ModInitializer entrypoint. Code here executes on both client and dedicated server environments and must not reference client-only classes.
chapter00.files.fabricRow1: Contains client-only Java source code, typically including ClientModInitializer, when split client sources are enabled.
chapter00.files.fabricRow2: Mod metadata descriptor declaring id, name, version, environment, entrypoints, depends, and mixins.
chapter00.files.fabricRow3: Client asset namespace directory under resources for translations, textures, and models; its name must match the mod ID.
chapter00.files.fabricRow4: Server data namespace directory for recipes, loot tables, and tags; create subdirectories as needed during development.
chapter00.files.fabricRow5: Mixin configuration listing Mixin classes and injection settings; client-only configurations may reside in src/client/resources.
chapter00.files.fabricRow6: Output directory generated by data-generation tasks. Modify the data generators and rerun generation rather than editing generated files manually.
chapter00.files.idReminder: Naming note: A mod ID may contain hyphens (for example, vocabulary-spark), whereas Java package names cannot contain hyphens (for example, vocabularyspark).
chapter00.files.buildBody: Build artifacts are written to build/libs. When distributing the mod, select the primary mod JAR rather than the accompanying sources JAR.
chapter00.habits.title: Development practices
chapter00.habits.intro: As a maintainable engineering convention, the mod ID, metadata accessors, logger, and shared utility methods can be centralized in a dedicated References utility class. Smaller projects may alternatively keep these members in the primary entrypoint class.
chapter00.habits.exampleIntro: The example below illustrates a complete References utility class with a private constructor to prevent instantiation. Add your project's package declaration and ensure MOD_ID matches the id field in fabric.mod.json.
chapter00.habits.row0: Unique mod identifier and resource namespace; reference this constant consistently throughout the codebase.
chapter00.habits.row1: The FabricLoader singleton instance used to query loaded mod containers and runtime environment information.
chapter00.habits.row2: Resolves the ModContainer matching MOD_ID; orElseThrow() fails immediately if no matching container is registered, surfacing ID mismatches early.
chapter00.habits.row3: Mod metadata descriptor used to derive MOD_NAME and MOD_VERSION without duplicating metadata strings.
chapter00.habits.row4: Shared Gson instance configured with pretty printing enabled and HTML character escaping disabled.

chapter00.habits.lifecycleBody: Static metadata fields are evaluated in declaration order when the class is first initialized, meaning even a call to fromPath() triggers the ModContainer lookup. Consequently, this class should only be invoked after Fabric has loaded mod metadata rather than in a standalone main() method. As a compile-time String constant, reading MOD_ID alone typically does not trigger class initialization.
chapter00.habits.constant: Because MOD_ID is a compile-time String constant, reading it alone generally does not initialize the class, unlike runtime static fields such as MOD_NAME and MOD_VERSION. To decouple resource-identifier helpers from runtime container state, separate fromPath() from metadata lookups.
chapter00.habits.annotationsBody: @NonNull from JSpecify (org.jspecify.annotations.NonNull) designates a non-null return type, while JetBrains' @Contract("_ -> new") specifies that normal execution always returns a newly allocated object. Both annotations inform static analysis and IDE inspections without performing runtime null checks.
chapter00.habits.versionBody: Minecraft 26.3 uses net.minecraft.resources.Identifier and its fromNamespaceAndPath factory method; older imports such as net.minecraft.util.Identifier or ResourceLocation do not apply. In addition, this example uses Log4j whereas the official template defaults to SLF4J—ensure that the matching Logger type is imported.
chapter00.finish.title: Chapter checklist
chapter00.finish.body: Upon completing this chapter, verify that the development client launches cleanly, Gradle builds succeed without error, and both file and console encodings are configured to UTF-8. The constants and helper methods in References will be used throughout subsequent chapters.
